explain.title: Asexual reproduction
explain.body: Asexual reproduction does not involve the fusion of gametes. Its offspring are genetically identical to the parent. Binary fission, budding, spore formation, and vegetative propagation are methods described in this section.

explain.title: Binary fission and budding
explain.body: In bacterial binary fission, DNA replicates, the copies move to opposite sides, and the cell separates to form two daughter bacteria. Protists such as Amoeba divide their nucleus before their cytoplasm. In budding, a part of the parent grows out as a bud; it may separate or remain attached. Yeast and hydra reproduce by budding.

explain.title: Spore formation
explain.body: Spores are thick-walled asexual reproductive cells. Fungi produce them in sac-like structures called sporangia. The sporangium releases mature spores, which germinate when conditions become favourable. Some bacteria form endospores inside the cell in unfavourable conditions.

explain.title: Vegetative propagation
explain.body: Vegetative propagation makes a new plant from a vegetative part (root, stem or leaf) of its parent. It takes less time than sexual reproduction, and its offspring are genetically identical to the parent. It may happen naturally or through human methods.

explain.title: Natural structures in plants
explain.body: Stolons grow horizontally above the ground; tubers are fleshy underground stems with eyes; rhizomes grow horizontally below ground; bulbs have fleshy leaves; and corms do not. Suckers are shoots from the base of a plant or its underground roots. Modified Bryophyllum leaves have buds at their margins that can grow into new plants.

mistakes: Do not confuse a stolon with a rhizome: a stolon grows above the ground, while a rhizome grows below it.
Do not call potato eyes roots; they are buds.
Do not say that a corm has fleshy leaves. A bulb has fleshy leaves; a corm does not.
Do not reverse the stages of binary fission: in Amoeba, the nucleus divides before the cytoplasm.
Do not say that spores germinate in unfavourable conditions; they germinate when conditions are favourable.
Do not confuse natural vegetative propagation, which happens on its own, with artificial propagation, in which humans use plant parts.

writtenQuestions.text: Describe the advantages and disadvantages of vegetative propagation.
modelAnswer: Vegetative propagation allows many new plants to be produced in a short time.

However, the offspring do not have genetic differences.
They are equally sensitive to environmental changes and prone to the same diseases or pests.

explain.title: Cutting

explain.title: Grafting
explain.body: Grafting joins a bud or small stem of one plant to the roots or stems of a second plant. It can combine beneficial characteristics of two plants and is used for many commercial fruit trees and ornamental plants.

steps.why: The flowering plant itself is the diploid generation that begins this cycle.
steps.text: The flowering plant is the diploid sporophyte generation.

steps.why: Meiosis halves the chromosome number to make haploid spores.
steps.text: The sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis.

steps.why: The male and female spores develop into their respective gametophytes.
steps.text: Microspores develop into pollen grains, which are the male gametophytes; a megaspore develops into the embryo sac, the female gametophyte.

steps.why: Pollination transfers pollen to the stigma, where the pollen tube can form.
steps.text: Pollination transfers pollen from an anther to a stigma.

steps.why: The pollen tube carries the two sperms to the embryo sac.
steps.text: The pollen tube grows towards the ovule and carries two sperms into the embryo sac.

steps.why: The two sperm fusions form the zygote and the endosperm-forming nucleus.
steps.text: One sperm fuses with the egg to form a zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form a triploid nucleus.

steps.why: These changes lead to a seed that can grow into the next sporophyte.
steps.text: The zygote develops into an embryo, the ovule becomes a seed, and the ovary becomes a fruit.

example.question: Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.
example.answer: The diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores; these develop into gametophytes that make gametes. Fertilization forms a zygote, which develops into the next sporophyte.

explain.title: Alternation of generations
explain.body: The major groups of plants have two type generations during sexual reproduction which come one after the other. These are sporophyte generation and gametophyte generation. The sporophyte generation produces spores which grow and make the new gametophyte generation. The gametophyte generation produces gametes which unite and make the new sporophyte generation. This phenomenon is called alternation of generations.

explain.title: Flower parts
explain.body: The four concentric whorls are calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens), and gynoecium (carpels). A stamen has an anther and a filament. A carpel has an ovary, style, and stigma.

explain.title: Male and female gametophytes
explain.body: The microspore undergoes mitosis and forms a pollen grain, the male gametophyte. The ovule contains a megaspore mother cell; after meiosis and further development, one megaspore forms the female gametophyte, or embryo sac.

explain.title: Pollination and double fertilization
explain.body: Pollination is the transfer of pollen grains from an anther to a stigma. The pollen tube carries two sperms into the embryo sac. One fuses with the egg to form a zygote, and the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form a triploid nucleus that develops into endosperm.

explain.title: Seed and fruit formation
explain.body: After fertilization, the zygote develops into an embryo and the triploid nucleus develops into endosperm tissue. The ovule matures into a seed and the ovary changes into a fruit.

mistakes: Do not confuse pollination with fertilization: pollination is pollen transfer from anther to stigma; fertilization is the fusion of gametes or nuclei.
Do not swap the male and female gametophytes: the pollen grain is male and the embryo sac is female.
Do not say both sperms fuse with the egg. One fuses with the egg and the other with the fusion nucleus.
Do not confuse the ovary and ovule after fertilization: the ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit.
Do not call the fusion nucleus triploid before sperm fusion; the sperm fuses with it to produce the triploid nucleus.
When describing embryo-sac development, include that only one of the four megaspores remains alive.

explain.title: Asexual reproduction
explain.body: Asexual reproduction needs one parent and does not involve the fusion of gametes. Binary fission in bacteria, budding in yeast, and spore formation in fungi are examples. The offspring are usually genetically similar to the parent.

explain.title: Spores and survival
explain.body: Fungi produce spores that can be dispersed and can germinate in suitable conditions. Some bacteria form thick-walled endospores in harsh conditions. Protective spores can remain dormant until conditions become favourable.

explain.title: Vegetative propagation
explain.body: New plants can grow from vegetative parts such as stems, roots or leaves. Runners and stolons grow above the ground; rhizomes, tubers, bulbs and corms are underground structures. People can also use methods such as cuttings, grafting and layering.

explain.title: Flower structure and gametophytes
explain.body: The four flower whorls are calyx (sepals), corolla (petals), androecium (stamens) and gynoecium or carpel (stigma, style and ovary). The pollen grain is the male gametophyte; the embryo sac inside the ovule is the female gametophyte.

explain.title: Fertilization and plant generations
explain.body: A pollen grain germinates on the stigma and forms a pollen tube that carries male gametes to the embryo sac. One male gamete fuses with the egg and the other with the fusion nucleus: this is double fertilization. The embryo develops in the seed, and the seed grows into a new sporophyte plant.

mistakes: Do not call a rhizome an aboveground stem: it is underground; a runner or stolon is aboveground.
Do not confuse the male and female gametophytes: pollen grain is male, and the embryo sac is female.
Do not say that the endosperm is diploid: it is triploid (3n) in flowering plants.
In double fertilization, one male gamete fuses with the egg, while the other fuses with the fusion nucleus; the egg is not fertilized by two male gametes.
When describing spore formation, distinguish survival in harsh conditions from germination, which occurs in suitable conditions.
For binary fission, do not omit DNA replication or the formation of two daughter bacteria.

notes.title: Types of Asexual Reproduction
notes.answer: Vegetative propagation is a method of asexual reproduction in plants in which a new plant is produced from the vegetative part (root, stem or leaf) of the parent plant.
notes.explanation: Asexual reproduction makes new organisms without the fusion of gametes. In plants, vegetative propagation makes a new plant from a root, stem, or leaf. Some plants also reproduce by binary fission, budding, or spores.
notes.simple: A new plant can grow from a part of its parent, such as a stem or leaf, without seeds.
examples: A potato can grow a new plant from the buds, called eyes, on its tuber.
A strawberry can form a new plant at a node on its stolon.
steps: Identify the method: binary fission, budding, spore formation, or vegetative propagation.
For vegetative propagation, name the plant part or structure involved.
Give the textbook example if the question asks for one.
notes.checkAnswer: A horizontal stem that grows above the ground.

notes.title: Growing plants from plant parts
notes.answer: Cutting grows a new plant from a cut piece of stem or root; grafting joins a bud or small stem of one plant to the roots or stems of another plant.
notes.explanation: Artificial propagation is when people grow new plants using parts of a plant, such as stems or roots. Cutting and grafting are two common methods. These methods can preserve useful characteristics, but the new plants have little genetic variation.
notes.simple: People can make new plants from plant parts instead of seeds. A piece can be planted, or parts of two plants can be joined.
examples: Roses and grapevines can be grown from stem cuttings.
Sweet potato can be grown from root cuttings.
steps: For cutting, cut a piece of stem or root from a plant and use it to grow a new plant.
For grafting, attach a bud or small stem of one plant to the roots or stems of a second plant.
Remember that grafting can combine beneficial characteristics of two plants.
Remember that vegetative propagation produces plants identical to the parent, so they share the same strengths and weaknesses.
notes.checkQuestion: What is one difference between cutting and grafting?
notes.checkAnswer: Cutting uses a cut piece of stem or root to grow a new plant. Grafting joins plant parts so they grow as one plant.

notes.title: Sexual Reproduction in Flowering Plants
notes.answer: The male gametophyte is the pollen grain, and the female gametophyte is the embryo sac.
notes.explanation: In flowering plants, the diploid sporophyte makes haploid spores. These grow into small gametophytes, which make gametes. After fertilization, a diploid zygote develops into a new sporophyte.
notes.simple: The plant makes spores, spores grow into tiny structures that make gametes, and the joined gametes start a new plant.
examples: A pollen grain is the male gametophyte.
The embryo sac is the female gametophyte.
steps: The diploid sporophyte produces haploid spores by meiosis.
Spores grow into haploid male and female gametophytes.
The male gametophyte makes sperms; the female gametophyte contains the egg and fusion nucleus.
Pollination transfers pollen from an anther to a stigma.
One sperm fuses with the egg to form a zygote; the other fuses with the fusion nucleus to form the endosperm nucleus.
The ovule becomes a seed and the ovary becomes a fruit.
notes.checkQuestion: What are the male and female gametophytes in flowering plants?
notes.checkAnswer: The pollen grain is the male gametophyte; the embryo sac is the female gametophyte.

notes.title: Reproduction in Plants: Main Ideas
notes.answer: The pollen tube carries the male gametes towards the embryo sac.
notes.explanation: Plants can reproduce without seeds by using spores or vegetative parts, and sexually by producing gametes in flowers. In flowering plants, pollen carries the male gametes and the ovule contains the female gametophyte. Fertilization forms a seed, which can grow into a new sporophyte plant.
notes.simple: A plant can make a new plant from a plant part, or make seeds after fertilization. Flowers help make the male and female cells needed for seed formation.
examples: A potato tuber can grow into a new potato plant.
A pollen tube carries male gametes to the embryo sac in an ovule.
steps: Identify whether reproduction is asexual or sexual.
For asexual reproduction, look for one parent and no fusion of gametes.
For sexual reproduction in flowering plants, follow pollen to the ovule.
Remember that fertilization forms the embryo and endosperm, and the ovule develops into a seed.
notes.checkQuestion: Which structure carries the male gametes from a pollen grain towards the embryo sac?
notes.checkAnswer: The pollen grain is the male gametophyte; the embryo sac is the female gametophyte.

written.text: Explain the lifecycle of flowering plants, focusing on the alternation between the gametophyte and sporophyte generations.

The male gametophyte forms male gametes, and the female gametophyte contains the egg cell and polar nuclei.

One male gamete fuses with the egg to form a diploid zygote; the other fuses with the polar nuclei to form triploid endosperm. This is double fertilization.
The zygote develops into an embryo; the ovule becomes a seed, which germinates to form a new sporophyte.

written.text: Describe how the female gametophyte (embryo sac) develops within the ovule of a flower.
modelAnswer: A diploid megaspore mother cell in the ovule undergoes meiosis and forms four haploid megaspores.
Usually three megaspores degenerate, leaving one functional megaspore.
The functional megaspore undergoes three mitotic divisions, forming eight haploid nuclei.
The nuclei arrange into a seven-celled embryo sac: an egg cell and two synergids at one end, three antipodal cells at the other end, and a central cell with two polar nuclei.

written.text: How do asexual and sexual reproduction contribute differently to genetic diversity of plant populations?
modelAnswer: Asexual reproduction involves one parent and usually produces genetically similar offspring.
It therefore creates little genetic variation in the population.
Sexual reproduction involves the fusion of gametes and combines genetic material.
It produces varied offspring and increases genetic diversity in the plant population.
